lessons.title: Basic tools for dismantling: wrenches, sockets, and cutting torches
lessons.body:
To dismantle a car safely and efficiently, you need the right tools. Start with a basic socket set: 1/4-inch drive for small bolts (8-12mm), 3/8-inch for most engine and body bolts (10-19mm), and 1/2-inch for stubborn suspension and chassis bolts (17-24mm). In Africa, many scrapyards use second-hand tools from markets like Kariakoo in Tanzania or Ladipo in Nigeria. Buy a set of combination wrenches (8-22mm) and a breaker bar for rusted nuts. Penetrating oil like WD-40 is essentialâspray and wait 10 minutes before turning.

For cutting, an angle grinder with a 4.5-inch cutting disc (1mm thick) is the most versatile tool. Use it to cut exhaust pipes, seized bolts, and body panels. Always wear safety goggles and gloves. A reciprocating saw (like a Sawzall) with a metal blade is faster for thick sections. If you have access to oxy-acetylene cutting torches, they cut through 10mm steel in seconds, but they are expensive and require training. In many African yards, a simple hacksaw with a 24-teeth-per-inch blade works for small pipes.

Lifting tools matter: a 2-ton hydraulic jack and axle stands are minimum. For engines, a engine hoist (cherry picker) is ideal, but a chain block and a strong tree branch can work in rural areas. Always support the vehicle on stands before crawling underneath.

Organize your tools in a bucket or a wooden box. Keep a magnetic tray for boltsâlosing a 14mm bolt can stop a job. For electrical connectors, a set of plastic trim removal tools (or a flat screwdriver wrapped in tape) prevents broken clips. A multimeter (cheap ones cost $10) helps test alternators and starters before removal. Finally, keep a notebook and marker to label parts as you goâthis saves hours later.

lessons.title: Removing high-demand parts: alternators, starters, and radiators
lessons.body:
Alternators, starters, and radiators are the fastest-selling used parts in African scrapyards. Learn to remove them without damage.

**Alternator:** Disconnect the battery negative terminal first. Remove the drive belt by loosening the tensioner (usually a 14mm or 17mm bolt). Unplug the electrical connector (press the tab) and remove the main power wire (10mm nut). Then remove the mounting boltsâtypically two 14mm bolts. If seized, apply penetrating oil and tap with a hammer. On Toyota Corollas (common in Africa), the alternator often comes out from the top after removing the air intake. Test with a multimeter: a good alternator should show 13.5-14.5 volts when spinning.

**Starter:** Disconnect the battery. Remove the negative cable from the starter solenoid (12mm or 13mm nut). Then remove the positive cable (also 12mm). Unbolt the starterâusually two 14mm boltsâand pull it out. On many Japanese cars, you may need to remove the intake manifold bracket. A starter that clicks but doesn't crank is often just worn brushes; you can sell it as a rebuildable core for $15-30.

**Radiator:** Drain the coolant into a bucket (1.5-2 gallons). Disconnect the upper and lower hoses (use pliers on the clamps). Remove the fan shroud (10mm bolts). Unbolt the radiator mounts (usually 10mm or 12mm). Lift it out carefullyâdo not bend the fins. A used radiator for a Toyota Hilux sells for $40-80 in Kenya or Ghana. Pressure test it with a radiator tester (or just fill with water and look for leaks).

Always label the bolts in a bag with the part name. Store alternators and starters indoors to prevent rust. Radiators should be stored upright, not flat, to avoid bending the core.

lessons.title: Extracting engines and transmissions for resale or rebuild
lessons.body:
Pulling an engine and transmission is the biggest job in a scrapyard, but it pays wellâa used Toyota 2E engine sells for $300-500 in West Africa, and a 5-speed manual gearbox for $150-250. Follow this method.

First, drain all fluids: engine oil (10-15 liters), coolant (5-7 liters), and transmission oil (2-3 liters). Remove the battery and the hood (bonnet). Label every wire and hose you disconnect with masking tape and a markerâtake photos with your phone if you have one. Disconnect the fuel lines (clamp them to prevent spillage), throttle cable, and all electrical connectors (injectors, sensors, alternator, starter). Remove the radiator and fan.

Support the transmission with a jack or a strong strap. Remove the driveshaft (4 bolts at the differential, 4 at the transmission). For front-wheel-drive cars, remove the CV axles (32mm nut at the hub, then pry out). Unbolt the engine mountsâusually two on the sides and one on the transmission. On a rear-wheel-drive car, you can pull the engine and transmission together as one unit. Use an engine hoist (cherry picker) rated at 1 ton. If no hoist, use a chain block and a sturdy tree branchâbut never get under the load.

Lift slowly, checking for anything still attached. Once out, separate the transmission from the engine (remove the bellhousing boltsâusually 6 to 8 bolts, 14mm or 17mm). Store the engine on a tire or wooden pallet, not directly on the ground. For rebuilds, sell the engine as a core if it has a blown head gasketârebuilders pay $100-200. A good running engine can be sold as-is. Keep the ECU and wiring harness with the engineâthey add value. Label the engine with its make, model, and year using a paint marker.

lessons.title: Salvaging interior components: seats, dashboards, and electronics
lessons.body:
Interior parts are lightweight, easy to remove, and sell quickly. A clean set of seats for a Toyota Hiace can fetch $80-150 in Uganda or Zambia. Dashboards, radios, and ECUs are also in demand.

**Seats:** Remove the four bolts holding each seat (usually 14mm or 17mm). For front seats, slide them back to access the rear bolts, then forward for the front. Disconnect any electrical connectors under the seat (for power seats or airbag sensors). Lift the seat outâtwo people make it easier. Check for tears or stains; clean with soap and water. Store seats indoors to prevent sun damage.

**Dashboards:** This is delicate. Remove the negative battery cable first. Take out the glovebox and lower panels (Phillips screws). Unbolt the steering column (4 bolts, 12mm) and lower it. Disconnect all wiring harnesses behind the dashboardâlabel them. Remove the radio (special tools or two U-shaped wires). The dashboard is held by 6-10 bolts (10mm) along the top and sides. Pull it out slowly; it may catch on the heater core. A cracked dashboard is still sellable for $20-50; a perfect one for $100+.

**Electronics:** The ECU (engine control unit) is usually behind the glovebox or under the passenger seat. Unplug it carefullyânever pull the wires. Radios, amplifiers, and speakers are easy to remove. Test them with a 12V battery before selling. Airbags are dangerousâdo not remove them unless you are trained; sell the car with airbags intact or call a professional. Keep small parts like knobs, switches, and fuses in labeled zip-lock bags. A complete interior from a popular car can earn you $200-400 if sold as a set.

lessons.title: Removing body panels, doors, and windows without damage
lessons.body:
Body panels, doors, and windows are high-value itemsâa used door for a Toyota Hilux sells for $100-200 in Nigeria, and a windshield for $50-150. But they damage easily. Follow these steps.

**Doors:** Open the door and remove the interior trim panel (clips or screws). Disconnect the wiring harness for the window motor, lock, and speakersâthere is usually a rubber boot between the door and body; pull it back and unplug the connector. Remove the door hinge bolts (usually 12mm or 14mm, two per hinge). Have a helper hold the door while you remove the last bolt. Never let it dropâbent hinges make the door worthless. Label the door with its position (front left, rear right) using masking tape.

**Body panels (fenders, hoods, bumpers):** For bolt-on panels, remove all bolts (10mm, 12mm, or 14mm). For welded panels, use a spot weld cutter (drill bit) or an angle grinder to cut the weldsâbut this damages the panel. Only do this if the panel is rare. For plastic bumpers, unclip the sides and remove the bolts underneath. Store panels flat or standing on edge, not leaning, to avoid warping.

**Windows:** For side windows, remove the door trim and unbolt the window regulator (3-4 bolts, 10mm). Slide the glass out. For windshields, use a windshield removal tool (a wire with handles) or a cold chisel and hammerâbut this often cracks the glass. A better method: use a utility knife to cut the urethane seal, then push the glass out from inside with your feet (wear shoes). Two people are needed. If the glass breaks, sweep up immediatelyâglass shards are dangerous. Sell windshields only if they have no cracks or chips. Store them upright in a rack with cardboard between them.

lessons.title: Organizing and labeling removed parts for easy inventory
lessons.body:
A disorganized scrapyard loses money. You forget what you have, parts get damaged, and customers leave because you can't find anything. A simple system fixes this.

**Labeling:** Use a permanent marker or paint pen to write on the part itselfâmake, model, year, and part name. For example: "Toyota Corolla 2005 Alternator". For small parts, put them in a zip-lock bag with a paper label inside. For bolts, tape them to the part or put them in a bag labeled with the part name. Never rely on memory.

**Shelving and storage:** Build wooden shelves or use metal racks (old bed frames work). Keep heavy parts (engines, transmissions) on the floor on pallets. Medium parts (alternators, starters, radiators) on middle shelves. Small parts (ECUs, sensors, bolts) in labeled plastic bins on top shelves. Group by system: engine parts together, transmission parts together, body parts together. For doors and panels, build a rack with vertical slotsâlike a file cabinetâso they don't fall.

**Inventory log:** Keep a notebook (or a simple Excel sheet on a phone) with columns: Part name, Make/Model, Year, Condition, Price, Location (shelf number). Update it every time you add or sell a part. In Africa, many successful scrapyards use a chalkboard on the wall listing high-demand parts and prices. Take photos of expensive parts and keep them on your phoneâyou can send them to customers via WhatsApp.

**Security and weather:** Cover engines and electronics with tarps to keep dust and rain off. Store alternators and starters indoors if possible. Use old engine oil to wipe bare metal partsâit prevents rust for months. Check your inventory monthly and re-label anything faded. A well-organized yard can double your sales because customers trust you and return.

quiz.q: What size socket drive is recommended for most engine and body bolts?
quiz.explanation: 3/8-inch drive sockets fit most 10-19mm bolts found on engines and body panels.

quiz.q: Before removing an alternator, what should you disconnect first?
quiz.explanation: Disconnecting the battery negative terminal prevents electrical shorts and sparks.

quiz.q: What is a common sign that a starter is rebuildable?
options: A) It clicks but doesn't crank
C) It has a broken casing
quiz.explanation: A clicking starter often has worn brushes or solenoid contacts, which can be rebuilt.

quiz.q: How should you store a radiator to prevent damage?
quiz.explanation: Storing upright prevents bending the delicate fins and core.

quiz.q: What should you do with the ECU when selling an engine?
options: A) Keep it with the engine
D) Give it to the buyer for free
quiz.explanation: The ECU and wiring harness add value and make the engine easier to install.

quiz.q: When removing a front-wheel-drive engine, what must you remove before pulling the engine?
quiz.explanation: CV axles connect the transmission to the wheels and must be removed to free the engine/transmission assembly.

quiz.q: What is the best way to label a part for inventory?
options: A) Write on it with a permanent marker
C) Put it in a pile with similar parts
D) Ask a coworker to remember
quiz.explanation: Permanent marker on the part ensures it can be identified later without relying on memory.

quiz.q: Which tool is safest for removing a windshield without breaking it?
quiz.explanation: A windshield removal wire cuts the urethane seal cleanly, reducing the chance of cracks.

quiz.q: What should you do before removing a dashboard?
quiz.explanation: Disconnecting the battery prevents electrical shorts when unplugging dashboard wiring.

quiz.q: How many bolts typically hold a car seat to the floor?
quiz.explanation: Most seats are held by four bolts, one at each corner of the seat frame.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to support a vehicle before crawling underneath?
options: A) Use a hydraulic jack only
quiz.explanation: Axle stands are designed to hold the vehicle securely and prevent it from falling.

quiz.q: Which part is most likely to be damaged if you let a door drop during removal?
quiz.explanation: Dropping a door bends the hinges, making it hard to align and reducing its resale value.

quiz.q: What should you do with bolts when removing a part?
options: A) Throw them in a bucket
B) Tape them to the part or bag and label
C) Put them in your pocket
D) Leave them on the ground
quiz.explanation: Labeling and keeping bolts with the part prevents loss and makes reassembly easier.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to cut a seized exhaust bolt?
options: B) Use an angle grinder with a cutting disc
quiz.explanation: An angle grinder with a 1mm cutting disc cuts through rusted bolts quickly and safely.

quiz.q: What voltage should a good alternator produce when running?
quiz.explanation: A healthy alternator charges at 13.5-14.5 volts to keep the battery charged.

quiz.q: When removing a radiator, what should you do with the coolant?
options: A) Drain it into a bucket
B) Let it spill on the ground
C) Leave it in the radiator
quiz.explanation: Coolant is toxic and should be collected for proper disposal or recycling.

quiz.q: What is a common price range for a used alternator in African scrapyards?
quiz.explanation: Used alternators typically sell for $15-30 depending on condition and demand.

quiz.q: How should you store engines to prevent damage?
options: A) On a tire or pallet
D) Stacked on top of each other
quiz.explanation: Storing on a tire or pallet keeps the engine off the ground, preventing rust and damage.

quiz.q: What is the first step when removing a dashboard?
quiz.explanation: Disconnecting the battery prevents electrical shocks and shorts when working on wiring.

quiz.q: Which interior part is most valuable if in good condition?
quiz.explanation: A perfect dashboard can sell for $100 or more, while other small parts fetch much less.

quiz.q: What tool is best for removing plastic trim without breaking clips?
quiz.explanation: Plastic trim tools are designed to pry clips without damaging them or the trim.

quiz.q: When removing a body panel that is welded, what tool do you use?
quiz.explanation: A spot weld cutter drills out the weld without destroying the panel.

quiz.q: What should you do with airbags when salvaging interior parts?
options: B) Leave them alone unless trained
quiz.explanation: Airbags can deploy unexpectedly and cause injury; only trained professionals should handle them.

quiz.q: How can you prevent rust on bare metal parts?
options: B) Wipe with old engine oil
D) Leave them in the rain
quiz.explanation: A thin coat of oil creates a barrier against moisture and rust.

quiz.q: What is a good way to keep an inventory of parts?
options: B) Notebook or Excel sheet with location
quiz.explanation: A written or digital log with part details and shelf location saves time and increases sales.

quiz.q: When removing a transmission, what should you support it with?
quiz.explanation: A jack or strap holds the transmission safely while you unbolt it.

quiz.q: What is the typical price for a used manual gearbox in West Africa?
quiz.explanation: A used 5-speed manual gearbox often sells for $150-250 depending on model and condition.

quiz.q: What should you do before removing a fuel line?
options: A) Clamp it to prevent spillage
B) Cut it with a grinder
quiz.explanation: Clamping the fuel line stops fuel from spilling and reduces fire risk.

quiz.q: How should you store windshields?
options: B) Upright in a rack with cardboard between
D) Stacked on top of each other
quiz.explanation: Upright storage with padding prevents scratches and breakage.

quiz.q: What is the best way to remove a door hinge bolt?
quiz.explanation: Door hinge bolts are typically 12mm or 14mm and require a socket or wrench.
